setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: In the ATLS primary survey, what is the correct order of priorities?

options.A: Exposure, circulation with haemorrhage control, airway, breathing and disability last
options.C: Airway with C-spine protection, breathing, circulation with haemorrhage control, disability, exposure
options.D: Breathing, circulation, airway with cervical spine protection, then exposure and finally disability
options.E: Disability, airway, breathing, circulation, exposure

explanation: ATLS prioritises threats by speed of lethality: airway with cervical spine restriction, breathing and ventilation, circulation with haemorrhage control, disability (neurological status) and exposure with environmental control. Many civilian and military systems now place catastrophic external haemorrhage control first (<C>ABC).
referenceText: ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: A hypotensive patient after a motorcycle crash has a positive FAST scan with free fluid in Morison's pouch and does not respond to initial transfusion. What is the next step?

options.E: Angiography of the mesenteric vessels

explanation: A positive FAST in a haemodynamically unstable non-responder indicates intra-abdominal haemorrhage requiring emergency laparotomy. CT is appropriate only for stable or transient responders. Moving unstable patients to the CT scanner is dangerous.
referenceText: ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: A hypotensive patient has an open-book pelvic fracture on radiograph. Where should a pelvic binder be applied?

options.C: Around the waist at the umbilicus
options.E: Over the lower ribs

explanation: Pelvic binders reduce pelvic volume and stabilise fracture fragments when placed at the level of the greater trochanters. Placement over the iliac crests is ineffective and may widen the fracture. Persistent haemorrhage is managed with angioembolisation or preperitoneal packing.
referenceText: ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]; Rossaint et al. 2023 (European trauma bleeding guideline, 6th ed.) [184]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: In a severely injured patient with hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy, what is the principle of damage control surgery?

options.B: An abbreviated operation to control bleeding and contamination, then ICU resuscitation and later repair
options.D: Delay surgery until coagulopathy is corrected
options.E: Definitive repair of all injuries in one prolonged operation, regardless of the patient's physiology

explanation: Damage control surgery limits operative time to essential steps (haemorrhage control, contamination control, temporary abdominal closure). ICU resuscitation corrects physiology, followed by planned return to theatre within 24–72 hours for definitive repair.
referenceText: ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]; Rossaint et al. 2023 (European trauma bleeding guideline, 6th ed.) [184]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: An elderly patient with multiple unilateral rib fractures has poor cough and falling vital capacity despite IV opioids. Which intervention most improves respiratory function?

options.B: Regional analgesia, e.g. thoracic epidural or a paravertebral or serratus plane catheter
options.E: Routine intubation and ventilation of all elderly patients with multiple unilateral rib fractures

explanation: Effective analgesia is the cornerstone of rib fracture management, enabling deep breathing and cough. Regional techniques improve pulmonary function and may reduce pneumonia and mortality in the elderly. Surgical rib fixation is considered in flail chest and selected patients.
referenceText: ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: After blunt chest trauma, a patient's oxygenation progressively worsens over 24 hours with patchy opacities that do not follow anatomical segments. What is the most likely diagnosis and key management principle?

options.A: Pulmonary contusion; avoid fluid overload, give analgesia and support ventilation
options.C: ARDS from sepsis; give high-dose steroids
options.E: Tension pneumothorax; insert a chest drain and repeat the chest radiograph in 6 hours

explanation: Pulmonary contusion evolves over 24–48 hours with alveolar haemorrhage and oedema. Management is supportive: analgesia, physiotherapy, judicious fluids and lung-protective ventilation if required. Steroids and prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated.
referenceText: ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: After a high-speed deceleration injury, a patient's chest radiograph shows a widened mediastinum. CT confirms a contained aortic isthmus injury. What is the most appropriate management?

options.B: Fluid loading to raise systolic BP above 140 mmHg before transfer for surgery
options.E: Strict heart rate and BP control (impulse control) with planned TEVAR

explanation: Blunt aortic injury most commonly occurs at the isthmus. Initial management aims to reduce aortic wall stress with beta-blockers and BP control (systolic below about 100–120 mmHg, heart rate below 80), followed by TEVAR, which has replaced open repair in most cases.
referenceText: ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]; Mazzolai et al. 2024 (ESC peripheral arterial and aortic diseases) [133]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: A patient with a stab wound to the left parasternal area has hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds. What is the most appropriate definitive treatment?

options.A: Needle pericardiocentesis as definitive treatment in the ED
options.B: Surgical exploration (sternotomy or thoracotomy) for cardiac repair
options.E: Chest drain insertion

explanation: Beck's triad (hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds) suggests tamponade from a cardiac wound. Pericardiocentesis may be a temporising measure, but definitive treatment is surgical repair. eFAST rapidly identifies pericardial fluid.
referenceText: ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: In which scenario is emergency department resuscitative thoracotomy most likely to be successful?

options.A: Blunt trauma with asystole after 30 minutes of CPR
options.C: Blunt trauma with no signs of life at the scene and prolonged transport
options.D: Penetrating chest trauma with loss of signs of life within 15 minutes of CPR
options.E: Isolated severe head injury

explanation: Survival after resuscitative thoracotomy is highest in penetrating thoracic injury (particularly stab wounds with tamponade) with short CPR duration (under 15 minutes). Outcomes after blunt trauma with prolonged CPR are very poor.
referenceText: ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: After blunt chest trauma, which screening approach is recommended for blunt cardiac injury?

options.A: ECG and troponin; if both normal, significant injury is unlikely
options.E: Coronary angiography in all patients with a sternal fracture or chest wall bruising

explanation: EAST guidelines recommend an admission ECG and troponin for suspected blunt cardiac injury; normal results essentially exclude significant injury. Abnormal ECG or troponin warrant monitoring and echocardiography for haemodynamic instability.
referenceText: ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: After blunt chest trauma, a patient has a pneumothorax with a persistent large air leak despite a correctly placed chest drain and failure of the lung to re-expand. What should be suspected?

options.E: Oesophageal rupture only; perform a contrast swallow

explanation: A large persistent air leak with non-expanding lung after trauma suggests tracheobronchial disruption. Bronchoscopy confirms the diagnosis. A second chest drain may be required, and surgical repair is often necessary; selective ventilation may be needed.
referenceText: ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]; Roberts et al. 2023 (BTS pleural disease) [180]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: A haemodynamically stable patient has a grade III splenic laceration on CT with a contrast blush. What is the preferred management?

options.C: Laparoscopic splenorrhaphy in all cases with a contrast blush
options.E: Discharge home

explanation: Haemodynamically stable patients with solid-organ injury are managed non-operatively, with angioembolisation for contrast extravasation (blush). Instability or peritonitis mandates surgery. Post-splenectomy (or major embolisation) patients need vaccination against encapsulated organisms.
referenceText: ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: After damage control laparotomy, a patient's abdomen is left open with temporary closure. What technique is suggested by WSACS to facilitate early fascial closure?

options.E: Routine use of mesh for primary closure in all patients

explanation: WSACS suggests negative pressure wound therapy for temporary abdominal closure, which manages fluid, reduces contamination and improves rates of early fascial closure. Early primary closure reduces complications such as enteroatmospheric fistula.
referenceText: Kirkpatrick et al. 2013 (WSACS abdominal compartment syndrome) [114]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: Which factor most commonly leads to under-triage of older trauma patients?

options.A: Blunted physiological response (e.g. beta-blockers) and anticoagulant-related bleeding
options.B: Higher heart rates in older patients
options.E: Lower rates of intracranial haemorrhage on anticoagulants than in younger trauma patients

explanation: Older patients have reduced physiological reserve, may not mount tachycardia (beta-blockers, pacemakers), and often take anticoagulants. A "normal" BP may represent shock. Lower thresholds for trauma team activation, CT imaging and anticoagulant reversal are recommended.
referenceText: ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]; Rockwood et al. 2005 (Clinical Frailty Scale) [182]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
topic: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: A man trapped under rubble for 6 hours is about to be extricated. Which intervention is most important before release?

options.B: Apply tourniquets to all limbs permanently
options.D: Delay all fluids until after hospital arrival, to avoid pulmonary oedema during transport
options.E: Start IV fluids before extrication to prevent hypovolaemia and hyperkalaemic arrest

explanation: Release of compression allows potassium, myoglobin and acids into the circulation and fluid sequestration into injured muscle, risking hypovolaemia, hyperkalaemic arrest and AKI. Early IV fluids, ideally before extrication, and cardiac monitoring are recommended.
referenceText: Bosch et al. 2009 (rhabdomyolysis) [22]; ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]
tags: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: A ventilated patient with a tibial fracture has a tense calf. The compartment pressure is 38 mmHg and diastolic BP is 60 mmHg. What is the appropriate management?

options.B: Elevate the limb above heart level and observe with hourly clinical examination and analgesia
options.D: Urgent fasciotomy: the perfusion gradient (diastolic minus compartment) is below 30 mmHg
options.E: Repeat pressure measurement in 24 hours

explanation: Compartment syndrome is clinical but difficult to assess in sedated patients. A difference between diastolic and compartment pressure (ΔP) below 30 mmHg indicates need for fasciotomy. Delays cause irreversible muscle and nerve necrosis and rhabdomyolysis.
referenceText: ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: A 70-kg man has 40% TBSA full- and partial-thickness burns. Using the Parkland formula, how much crystalloid is estimated for the first 8 hours from the time of injury?
explanation: Parkland: 4 mL × weight (kg) × %TBSA = 4 × 70 × 40 = 11,200 mL in 24 hours, half (5600 mL) in the first 8 hours from injury and the rest over 16 hours. ISBI recommends starting at 2–4 mL/kg/%TBSA and titrating to urine output to avoid fluid creep.
referenceText: ISBI 2016 (burn care guidelines) [100]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: What urine output target is commonly used to titrate burn fluid resuscitation in adults?

options.E: Urine output is not used

explanation: Hourly urine output of about 0.5 mL/kg/h in adults (higher with myoglobinuria) is the main endpoint. Over-resuscitation (fluid creep) causes abdominal and limb compartment syndromes, pulmonary oedema and conversion of burn depth; albumin may be used as rescue.
referenceText: ISBI 2016 (burn care guidelines) [100]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: An adult has partial- and full-thickness burns covering the entire back of the trunk, the whole right arm and the perineum. Using the rule of nines, what is the approximate TBSA burned?
explanation: Rule of nines (adult): posterior trunk 18%, each arm 9%, perineum 1%: total 28%. Superficial (epidermal) burns are excluded. The palm of the patient's hand (including fingers) represents about 1% TBSA for irregular burns.
referenceText: ISBI 2016 (burn care guidelines) [100]; ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: A patient rescued from an enclosed-space fire has facial burns, singed nasal hair, soot in the oropharynx, hoarseness and stridor. What is the most appropriate airway management?

options.A: Delay intubation until fluid resuscitation is complete and the extent of oedema is assessed
options.B: Tracheostomy in the emergency department in all cases
options.C: High-flow oxygen and nebulised salbutamol only
options.D: Observe and intubate only if SpO2 falls below 90%
options.E: Early intubation by an experienced operator with a large tube, before oedema progresses

explanation: Upper airway oedema worsens over hours, especially with resuscitation fluids. Hoarseness, stridor and respiratory distress indicate imminent obstruction; early intubation with a large tube (to permit bronchoscopy) is indicated. Uncut tubes are used to allow for facial swelling.
referenceText: ISBI 2016 (burn care guidelines) [100]; Higgs et al. 2018 (DAS/ICS critically ill intubation) [91]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: A ventilated patient with circumferential full-thickness burns of the chest has rising airway pressures and falling tidal volumes. What is the most appropriate intervention?

options.E: Increase tidal volume

explanation: Circumferential full-thickness burns form inelastic eschar that restricts chest wall expansion and ventilation, or limb perfusion. Escharotomy incisions through the eschar along mid-axillary and subcostal lines restore compliance.
referenceText: ISBI 2016 (burn care guidelines) [100]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: Which therapy reduces the hypermetabolic response after severe burns?

options.A: Avoiding enteral nutrition for 7 days to reduce metabolic rate and splanchnic oxygen demand
options.C: Propranolol to lower heart rate and energy expenditure, plus high-protein enteral feeding
options.E: Thyroid hormone supplementation

explanation: Severe burns produce prolonged hypermetabolism and catabolism. Early enteral feeding with high protein, early excision and grafting, environmental warming, propranolol and oxandrolone reduce muscle wasting and energy expenditure.
referenceText: ISBI 2016 (burn care guidelines) [100]; Singer et al. 2019 (ESPEN ICU nutrition) [199]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: Which strategy reduces infection and mortality in major full-thickness burns?

options.B: Delaying excision until eschar separates spontaneously
options.D: Prophylactic systemic antibiotics for all patients
options.E: Early excision and grafting (within the first few days)

explanation: Early excision of necrotic tissue with skin grafting or substitutes reduces infection, length of stay and mortality. Prophylactic systemic antibiotics are not recommended; topical antimicrobials and infection surveillance are used instead.
referenceText: ISBI 2016 (burn care guidelines) [100]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: A worker splashes hydrofluoric acid on his hand and has severe pain with little visible injury. Besides copious irrigation, what specific treatment is needed?

options.A: Topical calcium gluconate gel, regional calcium for severe pain, and monitoring for hypocalcaemia
options.E: Sodium bicarbonate infusion to neutralise absorbed fluoride ions and prevent severe systemic acidosis

explanation: Fluoride ions penetrate deeply, binding calcium and magnesium and causing severe pain, tissue necrosis and systemic hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia and hyperkalaemia with arrhythmias. Calcium gluconate (topical, subcutaneous, intra-arterial) neutralises fluoride.
referenceText: ISBI 2016 (burn care guidelines) [100]; Nelson et al. 2019 (Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies) [151]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: A ventilated, obtunded blunt trauma patient has a normal high-quality cervical spine CT. What does the EAST guideline recommend?

options.B: Keep the collar until the patient can be examined clinically, regardless of duration
options.D: Removal of the cervical collar based on the negative high-quality CT alone
options.E: MRI in all patients before collar removal

explanation: EAST conditionally recommends cervical collar removal in obtunded adults after a negative high-quality CT, because the risk of missed unstable injury is very low and prolonged collar use causes pressure ulcers, raised ICP, aspiration and airway difficulty.
referenceText: Patel et al. 2015 (EAST cervical collar clearance) [163]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: When should pharmacological VTE prophylaxis be started in a major trauma patient once bleeding is controlled?

options.B: Only if a DVT is detected on screening ultrasound at day 7 after admission
options.E: Within 24 hours of haemostasis, using LMWH when bleeding risk allows

explanation: Trauma patients have high VTE risk. European guidelines recommend mechanical prophylaxis early and pharmacological prophylaxis within 24 hours after bleeding has been controlled, including in stable TBI after a stable repeat CT. LMWH is preferred to UFH.
referenceText: Kahn et al. 2012 (ACCP VTE prevention, non-surgical) [108]; Rossaint et al. 2023 (European trauma bleeding guideline, 6th ed.) [184]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: Which variables make up the ABC score used to predict need for massive transfusion in trauma?

options.A: Penetrating mechanism, SBP ≤90 mmHg, HR ≥120/min and positive FAST
options.B: Age, GCS, lactate and base deficit
options.C: Respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, pain score and Glasgow Coma Scale
options.E: Haemoglobin, INR, fibrinogen and platelets

explanation: The ABC (Assessment of Blood Consumption) score assigns 1 point each for penetrating mechanism, systolic BP ≤90 mmHg, heart rate ≥120/min and positive FAST; a score of 2 or more predicts massive transfusion and can trigger a major haemorrhage protocol without laboratory results.
referenceText: Nunez et al. 2009 (ABC score) [154]; Rossaint et al. 2023 (European trauma bleeding guideline, 6th ed.) [184]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: Why is active prevention of hypothermia essential in haemorrhaging trauma patients?

options.A: Hypothermia has no effect on bleeding
options.B: Hypothermia reduces oxygen delivery requirements to zero, so it protects injured tissue
options.E: It impairs coagulation enzyme and platelet function, worsening bleeding and mortality

explanation: Hypothermia below 35 °C is associated with increased blood loss and mortality in trauma. Warming measures include warmed fluids and blood, forced-air warming, warm environment and limiting exposure.
referenceText: Rossaint et al. 2023 (European trauma bleeding guideline, 6th ed.) [184]; ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: A patient with extensive burns receives 18 L of crystalloid in 24 hours and develops oliguria, high airway pressures and bladder pressure of 28 mmHg. What is this condition called?

options.E: Primary abdominal compartment syndrome

explanation: Secondary ACS arises from conditions not originating in the abdomen, such as massive fluid resuscitation in burns, sepsis or pancreatitis. Primary ACS results from abdominal pathology (trauma, haemorrhage, surgery). Recurrent ACS develops after treatment of primary or secondary ACS.
referenceText: Kirkpatrick et al. 2013 (WSACS abdominal compartment syndrome) [114]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: A patient with a stab wound to the neck has an expanding haematoma, pulsatile bleeding and stridor. What is the appropriate management?

options.B: Probe the wound in the emergency department
options.C: Secure the airway and proceed to immediate operative exploration
options.D: CT angiography of the neck before any intervention
options.E: Discharge with antibiotics

explanation: "Hard signs" of vascular or aerodigestive injury (expanding or pulsatile haematoma, active bleeding, bruit, airway compromise, subcutaneous emphysema with stridor) mandate immediate surgery. Stable patients without hard signs are evaluated with CT angiography. Wound probing is dangerous.
referenceText: ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: After an explosion, a patient has hypoxaemia, haemoptysis and bilateral infiltrates without chest wall injury. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.E: Aspiration pneumonia

explanation: Primary blast injury affects air-containing organs (lungs, middle ear, bowel). Blast lung presents with hypoxaemia, haemoptysis and a "butterfly" pattern of infiltrates within hours. Management includes lung-protective ventilation, cautious fluids and vigilance for barotrauma and air embolism.
referenceText: ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: In a bleeding trauma patient with life-threatening hypotension despite blood product resuscitation, what does the European guideline suggest?

options.C: Large-volume crystalloid infusion until the MAP reaches 90 mmHg
options.D: Phenylephrine boluses as the only treatment
options.E: Noradrenaline may be added to fluids to maintain target pressure

explanation: The European guideline recommends vasopressors (noradrenaline) in addition to fluids to maintain target arterial pressure in life-threatening hypotension, and inotropes for myocardial dysfunction. Haemorrhage control and blood products remain the priority.
referenceText: Rossaint et al. 2023 (European trauma bleeding guideline, 6th ed.) [184]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
topic: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: After a left-sided stab wound to the lower chest, a stable patient has a normal CT. Why may diagnostic laparoscopy still be indicated?

options.B: Small diaphragmatic injuries are often missed on CT and can later herniate
options.D: To diagnose pulmonary contusion and small haemothoraces that CT commonly misses
options.E: To exclude aortic injury

explanation: Left thoracoabdominal penetrating injuries carry a risk of diaphragmatic laceration that CT may miss. Diagnostic laparoscopy identifies and repairs these injuries, preventing delayed herniation of abdominal viscera.
referenceText: ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]
tags: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: What should be arranged for a patient after emergency trauma splenectomy?

options.B: Pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib vaccination, plus education on prompt antibiotics
options.D: Routine iron supplementation and lifelong low-dose aspirin to prevent thrombocytosis
options.E: No specific measures

explanation: Asplenic patients are at lifelong risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection from encapsulated organisms. Vaccination (ideally about 14 days after emergency splenectomy or before discharge), annual influenza vaccination, prophylactic or standby antibiotics and patient education are recommended.
referenceText: ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: On day 5 after colorectal anastomosis, a patient develops tachycardia, fever, ileus and rising CRP, then becomes hypotensive. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Wait for CRP to exceed 300 mg/L
options.C: Resuscitation, antibiotics and urgent CT with source control (drainage or relaparotomy)
options.E: Start total parenteral nutrition only and rest the bowel for 7 days before any imaging

explanation: Anastomotic leak typically presents 5–8 days after surgery. Tachycardia, rising inflammatory markers and failure to progress are early warnings. Septic shock requires prompt resuscitation, antibiotics and source control; delay increases mortality.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: A patient with 50% TBSA burns develops sepsis on day 10 with green discoloration and rapid conversion of wounds. Which organism is most likely?

options.E: Listeria monocytogenes

explanation: Burn wound infection with P. aeruginosa may cause green exudate, dark discoloration and wound conversion. Burn patients are also prone to MRSA, Acinetobacter and fungal infections. Management includes debridement, topical antimicrobials and systemic antibiotics guided by cultures.
referenceText: ISBI 2016 (burn care guidelines) [100]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: During burn resuscitation, fluid requirements exceed 6 mL/kg/%TBSA at 12 hours. Which intervention is commonly used to reduce further crystalloid requirements?

options.B: Give furosemide to increase urine output
options.E: Stop all fluids for 6 hours

explanation: When fluid requirements exceed predicted values (fluid creep), albumin infusion can restore intravascular oncotic pressure and reduce total crystalloid volume and complications such as abdominal compartment syndrome. Diuretics invalidate urine output as an endpoint.
referenceText: ISBI 2016 (burn care guidelines) [100]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: A patient with smoke inhalation is conscious with COHb 18% and SpO2 98%. What is the most important immediate oxygen therapy?

options.B: Hyperbaric oxygen only if COHb exceeds 50%
options.C: Oxygen titrated to SpO2 94% using standard pulse oximetry
options.D: Room air to avoid oxygen toxicity
options.E: 100% oxygen via a tight-fitting non-rebreather mask or ventilator

explanation: High-concentration oxygen reduces the half-life of COHb from about 4–6 hours on air to about 60–90 minutes. Pulse oximetry overestimates oxygenation in CO poisoning, so it cannot guide therapy. Hyperbaric oxygen is considered for severe features.
referenceText: Weaver 2009 (carbon monoxide poisoning) [232]; ISBI 2016 (burn care guidelines) [100]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: After fasciotomy for compartment syndrome, which laboratory parameter should be monitored closely in the first 24 hours?

options.B: Potassium and creatine kinase, with renal function
options.D: Serum amylase and lipase every 6 hours after surgery
options.E: Serum ammonia

explanation: Reperfusion of ischaemic muscle releases potassium, myoglobin and acids, risking hyperkalaemia, arrhythmias and AKI. Close monitoring of potassium, CK, renal function and urine output is required, with fluids and treatment of hyperkalaemia.
referenceText: Bosch et al. 2009 (rhabdomyolysis) [22]; ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: Why is permissive hypotension avoided in bleeding trauma patients with severe TBI?

options.A: Hypotension lowers cerebral perfusion pressure, worsening secondary injury
options.B: TBI patients cannot receive blood products
options.C: Hypotension increases ICP directly by causing reflex cerebral vasodilatation and oedema
options.E: TBI patients do not bleed

explanation: In TBI, a single episode of hypotension doubles mortality. European guidelines recommend a MAP of 80 mmHg or more in patients with severe TBI, rather than the permissive targets used for other bleeding trauma patients.
referenceText: Rossaint et al. 2023 (European trauma bleeding guideline, 6th ed.) [184]; Carney et al. 2017 (Brain Trauma Foundation, 4th ed.) [31]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: A seat-belted driver has an abdominal wall seat-belt sign and a Chance fracture of L1. CT shows free fluid without solid-organ injury. What injury should be suspected?

options.E: Diaphragmatic rupture only, with gastric herniation

explanation: Seat-belt signs and flexion–distraction (Chance) fractures are associated with bowel and mesenteric injuries. Free fluid without solid-organ injury on CT raises suspicion; serial examination or laparoscopy/laparotomy may be required because early CT can miss bowel injury.
referenceText: ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: When should enteral nutrition ideally begin in a patient with major burns?

options.B: Only when bowel sounds are present
options.E: Only parenteral nutrition is appropriate

explanation: Early enteral feeding attenuates hypermetabolism, preserves gut integrity, reduces infections and improves wound healing. Protein requirements are high (1.5–2 g/kg/day). Parenteral nutrition is reserved for enteral failure.
referenceText: ISBI 2016 (burn care guidelines) [100]; Singer et al. 2019 (ESPEN ICU nutrition) [199]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: An elderly patient on warfarin (INR 3.0) has a traumatic subdural haematoma. What is the immediate management?

options.A: Rapid reversal with four-factor PCC and IV vitamin K
options.C: Withhold reversal unless the haematoma expands
options.E: Platelet transfusion

explanation: Anticoagulant-associated traumatic intracranial haemorrhage requires rapid reversal to prevent expansion. 4F-PCC acts faster than FFP, with IV vitamin K for sustained effect. Reversal should not wait for evidence of expansion.
referenceText: Rossaint et al. 2023 (European trauma bleeding guideline, 6th ed.) [184]; Tomaselli et al. 2020 (ACC oral anticoagulant bleeding pathway) [214]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: After a complete thoracic spinal cord injury, a patient has flaccid paralysis, areflexia and absent bulbocavernosus reflex below the level of injury, with normal blood pressure. What does this represent?

options.C: Permanent lower motor neurone injury in all cases, with no chance of any neurological recovery
options.E: Spinal shock: temporary loss of reflexes below the injury, not itself implying hypotension

explanation: Spinal shock describes transient loss of spinal reflexes below the level of injury, resolving over days to weeks with return of reflexes and later spasticity. Neurogenic shock refers to haemodynamic instability (hypotension, bradycardia) from loss of sympathetic tone, typically with injuries above T6.
referenceText: Walters et al. 2013 (AANS/CNS acute spinal cord injury) [231]; ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: In a crush injury patient with myoglobinuria and urine output of 50 mL/h after initial fluids, what is the target urine output?

options.C: About 200–300 mL/h (around 3 mL/kg/h) until myoglobinuria clears
options.E: No target; restrict IV fluids to avoid pulmonary oedema and compartment syndrome

explanation: High urine flow dilutes and clears myoglobin and reduces cast formation. Targets of about 200–300 mL/h are commonly used in established myoglobinuria, with careful monitoring for compartment syndrome and fluid overload, particularly if AKI develops.
referenceText: Bosch et al. 2009 (rhabdomyolysis) [22]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: Which laboratory markers does the European guideline recommend to estimate and monitor the extent of bleeding and shock?

options.E: Troponin

explanation: Lactate and base deficit are sensitive markers of hypoperfusion and the extent of haemorrhagic shock, and their trends guide resuscitation. A single haemoglobin value is a poor marker of early blood loss because of haemoconcentration.
referenceText: Rossaint et al. 2023 (European trauma bleeding guideline, 6th ed.) [184]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: A patient has life-threatening arterial bleeding from a traumatic thigh amputation. What is the most appropriate immediate measure?

options.C: Apply a tourniquet proximal to the wound
options.D: Insert an IV line before any haemorrhage control
options.E: Elevate the leg and wait for clotting

explanation: For life-threatening external limb haemorrhage, a tourniquet applied tightly proximal to the wound controls bleeding and saves lives. Haemostatic dressings and direct pressure are used for junctional wounds. Tourniquet time should be recorded.
referenceText: ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]; Rossaint et al. 2023 (European trauma bleeding guideline, 6th ed.) [184]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: Which patient is the most appropriate candidate for surgical stabilisation of rib fractures?

options.B: A patient with rib fractures and well-controlled pain on oral analgesia
options.C: A patient with flail chest failing to wean from ventilation
options.D: A patient with isolated sternal contusion
options.E: A patient with a single non-displaced rib fracture

explanation: Surgical rib fixation is considered in flail chest, particularly with ventilator dependence, severe chest wall deformity or uncontrolled pain. It may reduce ventilation days, pneumonia and tracheostomy in selected patients.
referenceText: ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: Which burn requires referral to a specialised burns centre?

options.A: Partial-thickness burns >10% TBSA, or burns of face, hands, perineum or major joints
options.B: A 1% superficial burn of the forearm
options.C: A small blister on the leg
options.E: A 2% superficial partial-thickness burn on the thigh in a previously healthy young adult

explanation: Burns centre referral criteria include partial-thickness burns over 10% TBSA in adults, full-thickness burns, burns to special areas (face, hands, feet, genitalia, perineum, major joints), electrical and chemical burns, inhalation injury and burns in patients with significant comorbidity.
referenceText: ISBI 2016 (burn care guidelines) [100]

setTitle: Trauma, Burns and Surgical Critical Care
stem: A patient with a pelvic fracture has blood at the urethral meatus and a scrotal haematoma. What should be done before urinary catheterisation?

options.A: Retrograde urethrography to exclude urethral injury
options.C: Perform cystoscopy under general anaesthesia immediately
options.D: Insert a urinary catheter with force if resistance is met
options.E: Insert a suprapubic catheter blindly without imaging

explanation: Blood at the meatus, perineal or scrotal haematoma, or a high-riding prostate suggest urethral injury, typically associated with pelvic fractures. A retrograde urethrogram should precede catheterisation, because blind catheter insertion can convert a partial into a complete tear. Suprapubic catheterisation is used if injury is confirmed.
referenceText: ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]
